verses.1:1: The Song of Songs, which belongs to Solomon.
verses.1:2: May he kiss me with kisses of his mouth, for your caresses are better than wine.
verses.1:3: In fragrance your oils are pleasing; your name is oil poured out; therefore young women love you.
verses.1:4: Draw me; let us run after you! The king has brought me into his chambers. Let us exult and be glad in you; let us praise your caresses more than wine. Rightly they love you.
verses.1:5: I am dark and lovely, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon.
verses.1:6: Do not stare at me because I am darkened, because the sun has scorched me. The sons of my mother grew angry with me; they set me to guard the vineyards, yet my own vineyard I have not guarded.
verses.1:7: Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you shepherd your flock, where you let it lie down at midday; for why should I be like one who veils herself beside the flocks of your companions?
verses.1:8: If you do not know for yourself, most beautiful of women, go out in the tracks of the flock and tend your young goats beside the dwellings of the shepherds.
verses.1:9: I have likened you, my companion, to a mare among the chariots of Pharaoh.
verses.1:10: Your cheeks are lovely with circlets, your neck with strings of beads.
verses.1:11: We will make for you circlets of gold, with studs of silver.
verses.1:12: While the king was at his table, my nard gave its fragrance.
verses.1:13: A sachet of myrrh is my beloved to me; between my breasts he spends the night.
verses.1:14: A cluster of henna is my beloved to me, in the vineyards of En-gedi.
verses.1:15: Look, you are beautiful, my companion; look, you are beautiful! Your eyes are doves.
verses.1:16: Look, you are beautiful, my beloved, indeed pleasant! Indeed, our couch is lush.
verses.1:17: The beams of our houses are cedar; our paneling is cypress.
verses.2:1: I am a crocus of Sharon, a lily of the valleys.
verses.2:2: Like a lily among the thorns, so is my companion among the daughters.
verses.2:3: Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. In his shade I delighted to sit, and his fruit was sweet to my palate.
verses.2:4: He brought me to the house of wine, and his banner over me is love.
verses.2:5: Strengthen me with raisin cakes, revive me with apples, for I am lovesick.
verses.2:6: His left arm is beneath my head, and his right arm embraces me.
verses.2:7: I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or by the does of the field: do not rouse or stir up love until it desires.
verses.2:8: The voice of my beloved! Look, here he comes, leaping across the mountains, springing across the hills.
verses.2:9: My beloved resembles a gazelle or a young stag. Look, here he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, peering through the lattices.
verses.2:10: My beloved answered and said to me, "Rise up, my companion, my beautiful one, and come away.
verses.2:11: For look, the winter has passed; the rain is over, gone its way.
verses.2:12: The blossoms have appeared in the land; the time of singing has arrived, and the turtledove's voice is heard in our land.
verses.2:13: The fig tree has ripened its early figs, and the vines in blossom give fragrance. Rise up, my companion, my beautiful one, and come away.
verses.2:14: My dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hiding place of the cliff, show me your appearance, let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet, and your appearance is lovely."
verses.2:15: Catch for us foxes, little foxes that ruin vineyards, while our vineyards are in blossom.
verses.2:16: My beloved belongs to me, and I belong to him; he is the one who pastures among the lilies.
verses.2:17: Until the day breathes and the shadows take flight, turn around, my beloved, be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of Bether.
verses.3:1: On my bed during the nights, I sought the one whom my soul loves; I sought him, yet I did not find him.
verses.3:2: "Let me rise now and go around in the city, in the streets and in the squares; let me seek the one whom my soul loves." I sought him, yet I did not find him.
verses.3:3: The watchmen who go around in the city found me. "Have you seen the one whom my soul loves?"
verses.3:4: Barely had I passed beyond them when I found the one whom my soul loves. I took hold of him and would not release him until I brought him to the house of my mother, and into the chamber of the one who conceived me.
verses.3:5: I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or by the does of the field: do not rouse or stir up love until it desires.
verses.3:6: Who is this ascending from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the powders of a merchant?
verses.3:7: Look, it is Solomon's litter! Sixty warriors are around it, from the warriors of Israel.
verses.3:8: All of them hold swords, trained in warfare, each man with his sword at his thigh against terror during the nights.
verses.3:9: King Solomon made a palanquin for himself from the trees of Lebanon.
verses.3:10: He made its pillars of silver, its backrest of gold, its seat of purple; its interior is inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.
verses.3:11: Go out and look, daughters of Zion, at King Solomon, at the crown with which his mother crowned him on his wedding day, and on the day of his heart's joy.
verses.4:1: Look, you are beautiful, my companion; look, you are beautiful! Your eyes are doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats gliding down from Mount Gilead.
verses.4:2: Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes coming up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, with not a bereaved one among them.
verses.4:3: Like a thread of scarlet are your lips, and your speech is lovely. Like a slice of pomegranate is your cheek behind your veil.
verses.4:4: Like the tower of David is your neck, built in tiers; a thousand shields hang on it, all the bucklers of the warriors.
verses.4:5: Your two breasts are like two fawns, a gazelle's twins, grazing among the lilies.
verses.4:6: Until the day breathes and the shadows take flight, I will make my way to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.
verses.4:7: You are wholly beautiful, my companion, and no blemish is in you.
verses.4:8: With me from Lebanon, my bride, come with me from Lebanon! Descend from the summit of Amana, from the summit of Senir and Hermon, from dens of lions, from mountains of leopards.
verses.4:9: You have taken my heart, my sister, my bride; you have taken my heart with one of your eyes, with one pendant of your necklace.
verses.4:10: How beautiful are your caresses, my sister, my bride! How much better are your caresses than wine, and the scent of your oils than all spices!
verses.4:11: Your lips drip honey from the comb, my bride; honey and milk are beneath your tongue, and the scent of your garments is like the scent of Lebanon.
verses.4:12: A locked garden is my sister, my bride, a locked spring, a sealed fountain.
verses.4:13: Your shoots are a pomegranate orchard with precious fruits, henna with spikenard,
verses.4:14: spikenard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all frankincense trees, myrrh and aloes, with all the foremost spices.
verses.4:15: A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and running streams from Lebanon.
verses.4:16: Awake, north wind, and come, south wind! Blow across my garden; let its spices flow forth. May my beloved come into his garden and eat its precious fruits.
verses.5:1: I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, companions; drink, and be drunk, lovers!
verses.5:2: I was sleeping, yet my heart was awake. The sound of my beloved knocking: "Open to me, my sister, my companion, my dove, my flawless one! For my head is filled with dew, my locks with the drops of night."
verses.5:3: I have taken off my tunic; how can I put it on? I have washed my feet; how can I soil them?
verses.5:4: My beloved stretched out his hand through the opening, and my inward parts stirred for him.
verses.5:5: I myself rose to open for my beloved, and my hands dripped myrrh, and my fingers flowing myrrh, onto the handles of the lock.
verses.5:6: I myself opened for my beloved, yet my beloved had slipped away and passed on. My soul went out when he spoke. I sought him, yet I did not find him; I called him, yet he did not answer me.
verses.5:7: The guards who go around in the city found me; they struck me, they wounded me; they took my wrap off me, the guards of the walls.
verses.5:8: I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem: if you find my beloved, what will you tell him? That I am sick with love.
verses.5:9: What is your beloved above any other beloved, most beautiful among women? What is your beloved above any other beloved, that you have made us swear like this?
verses.5:10: My beloved is gleaming and ruddy, standing out above ten thousand.
verses.5:11: His head is choice, fine gold; his locks are in waves, black as the raven.
verses.5:12: His eyes are like doves by streams of water, bathing in milk, perched by a brimming pool.
verses.5:13: His cheeks are like a bed of spice, towers of fragrant herbs; his lips are lilies, dripping with flowing myrrh.
verses.5:14: His hands are cylinders of gold, inlaid with beryl; his belly is smooth ivory, covered with sapphires.
verses.5:15: His legs are pillars of marble, founded on sockets of fine gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, select as the cedars.
verses.5:16: His mouth is all sweetness, and all of him is delight. This is my beloved, and this is my companion, daughters of Jerusalem.
verses.6:1: Where did your beloved go, most beautiful among women? Where did your beloved turn, so we may seek him with you?
verses.6:2: My beloved went down to his garden, to the beds of spice, to graze in the gardens and to pick lilies.
verses.6:3: I belong to my beloved, and my beloved belongs to me, he who grazes among the lilies.
verses.6:4: You are beautiful, my companion, like Tirzah, lovely like Jerusalem, awe-inspiring as armies with banners.
verses.6:5: Turn your eyes away from me, for they have overpowered me. Your hair is like a flock of goats gliding down from Gilead.
verses.6:6: Your teeth are like a flock of ewes coming up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, with not a bereaved one among them.
verses.6:7: Like a slice of pomegranate is your cheek behind your veil.
verses.6:8: Sixty queens there are, and eighty concubines, and young women without number.
verses.6:9: One alone is she, my dove, my flawless one; one alone is she to her mother, pure is she to the one who bore her. Daughters saw her and pronounced her blessed; queens and concubines, and they praised her.
verses.6:10: Who is this looking out like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, pure as the sun, awe-inspiring as armies with banners?
verses.6:11: I went down to the nut garden to look at the fresh shoots of the valley, to see if the vine had budded, if the pomegranates had bloomed.
verses.6:12: Before I knew it, my soul placed me in the chariots of my noble people.
verses.7:1: Turn back, turn back, Shulammite; turn back, turn back, so that we may gaze on you! Why do you gaze on the Shulammite as on the dance of the two camps?
verses.7:2: How lovely are your feet in sandals, daughter of a noble! The curves of your thighs are like ornaments, the work of the hands of an artisan.
verses.7:3: Your navel is a rounded basin; may it not lack blended wine. Your belly is a mound of wheat, hedged in with lilies.
verses.7:4: Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a female gazelle.
verses.7:5: Your neck is like a tower of ivory; your eyes are pools in Heshbon beside the gate of Bath-rabbim. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, looking out toward Damascus.
verses.7:6: Your head upon you is like Carmel, and the flowing hair of your head is like purple; a king is bound in the tresses.
verses.7:7: How lovely and how pleasant you are, love, in delights!
verses.7:8: This stature of yours resembles a palm tree, and your breasts are like clusters.
verses.7:9: I said, "I will climb a palm tree; I will grasp its fruit stalks." Now may your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the aroma of your breath like apples.
verses.7:10: And your palate is like the finest wine, flowing smoothly for my beloved, gliding over the lips of those who sleep.
verses.7:11: I belong to my beloved, and his longing is toward me.
verses.7:12: Come, my beloved, let us go out to the field; let us stay the night in the villages.
verses.7:13: Let us rise early to go to the vineyards; let us see if the vine has budded, if the blossom has opened, if the pomegranates have bloomed. There I will give my love to you.
verses.7:14: The mandrakes give off fragrance, and at our doorways are all kinds of choice fruits, new as well as old; my beloved, I have stored them up for you.
verses.8:1: If only you were like a brother to me, one who nursed at the breasts of my mother! If I found you outside, I would kiss you, and yet no one would scorn me.
verses.8:2: I would lead you, I would bring you into the house of my mother, she who used to teach me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, from the fresh juice of my pomegranate.
verses.8:3: May his left hand be beneath my head, and may his right hand embrace me.
verses.8:4: I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem: do not rouse and do not awaken love until it desires.
verses.8:5: Who is this coming up out of the wilderness, leaning against her beloved? Beneath the apple tree I awakened you; there your mother was in labor with you, there she who gave birth to you was in labor.
verses.8:6: Place me like a seal on your heart, like a seal on your arm; for love is as mighty as death, jealousy is as relentless as Sheol. Its bolts are bolts of fire, a flame of the LORD.
verses.8:7: Many waters cannot extinguish love, and rivers will not wash it away. If a man should give all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned.
verses.8:8: We have a young sister, and she has no breasts. What will we do for our sister on the day she is spoken for?
verses.8:9: If she is a wall, we will build a turret of silver upon her; and if she is a door, we will barricade her with a board of cedar.
verses.8:10: I am a wall, and my breasts are like towers; then in his eyes I became like one finding peace.
verses.8:11: A vineyard belonged to Solomon at Baal-hamon; he gave the vineyard over to keepers; each man was to bring a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.
verses.8:12: My vineyard, my own, is before me; the thousand is yours, Solomon, and two hundred are for those who keep its fruit.
verses.8:13: You who dwell in the gardens, companions are listening attentively to your voice; let me hear it!
verses.8:14: Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon mountains of spices.

notes.1:3: Hebrew wordplay links shemen ("oil") and shemekha ("your name"). The verb turaq ("poured out") is a 3fs Hophal form from riq, treating the normally masculine noun shemen as feminine here.
notes.1:4: The plural noun mesharim literally means "uprightness" or "straightness"; it is taken adverbially here ("rightly"), though some read it as an abstract subject ("the upright").
notes.1:7: The Masoretic Text reads ke'otyah, the feminine active participle of atah ("wrap/veil oneself"), rendered "like one who veils herself"; several ancient versions reflect a transposed root meaning "wandering."
notes.1:17: The Ketiv reads rchytnw (with chet), while the translated Qere reads rahitenu ("our paneling" or "our rafters," a hapax legomenon). Berotim is an Aramaicized spelling of Hebrew beroshim ("cypresses").
notes.2:1: Chavatstselet (traditionally rendered "rose") refers to a coastal wildflower of the Sharon plain, likely a crocus, narcissus, or asphodel.
notes.2:7: In Hebrew oath syntax, the conditional particle im ("if") expresses a strong prohibition ("do not..."). The 3fs verb techpats ("it desires") agrees with the feminine noun ha'ahavah ("love").
notes.2:12: The noun hazamir can mean either "singing" (from zamar II, matching the turtledove's voice) or "pruning" (from zamar I, referring to spring vine pruning).
notes.2:13: The Ketiv reads lky (an archaic or dialectal 2fs suffix form), whereas the translated Qere reads the standard form lakh ("for yourself"), idiomatic with the imperative "Rise up."
notes.2:17: Harey vater may denote a proper place name ("mountains of Bether") or be descriptive ("cleft/divided mountains," from the root batar, "to cut in two").
notes.3:6: The question mi zot ("Who is this") uses the feminine demonstrative zot, anticipating either the bride or the feminine noun mittah ("litter," v. 7). Avqat ("powder") is a hapax legomenon related to avaq ("dust").
notes.3:8: Achuzei cherev is literally a Qal passive participle construct ("grasped of sword"), a Hebrew idiom for men armed with or holding swords.
notes.3:9: Appiryon ("palanquin") is a hapax legomenon denoting an ornate portable royal carriage or covered litter, likely a foreign loanword.
notes.3:10: Refidato ("its backrest") is a hapax legomenon from rafad ("spread out/support"). The striking phrase ratsuf ahavah ("inlaid with love") is translated directly from the Masoretic Text.
notes.4:1: The verb galash, rendered gliding down, occurs only here and in 6:5 and describes the undulating movement of a flock descending a slope; tsammah, rendered veil, is also sometimes understood as locks or braids.
notes.4:3: The noun midbar, rendered speech, is a hapax legomenon from dabar, to speak, and can denote either speech or the mouth as the organ of speech; raqqah, rendered cheek, properly denotes the temple or side of the face.
notes.4:4: The word talpiyyot, rendered tiers, is a hapax legomenon of uncertain meaning, variously understood as courses of stone, weapons or an armory, or battlements.
notes.4:9: The ketiv reads masculine b'hd while the qere reads feminine be'achat, one, to agree with feminine ayin, eye, which is followed here; with one of your eyes idiomatically suggests a single glance. The verb libbavtini, you have taken my heart, is a denominative Piel from levav, heart.
notes.4:12: The Masoretic Hebrew reads gal, spring or fountain, parallel to ma'yan, rather than repeating gan, garden, as in the Septuagint and Vulgate.
notes.5:1: The plural dodim, rendered lovers, may be read either as a vocative parallel to re'im, companions, or adverbially as be drunk with love or caresses.
notes.5:4: Hebrew me'ay, my inward parts, idiomatically denotes the seat of deep emotion; alav, for him, follows the Masoretic Text rather than the variant within me reflected in the Septuagint.
notes.5:6: Hebrew nafshi yats'ah, my soul went out, is an idiom for fainting or despair; bedabbero, when he spoke, is the Piel infinitive construct of dabar, speak, with a third masculine singular suffix.
notes.5:12: The noun mille't, rendered brimming pool, is a hapax legomenon from male', be full, understood either as a full water basin parallel to streams of water or as a gemstone setting as in Exodus 28:17.
notes.5:13: The Masoretic vocalization reads migdelot, towers or raised mounds, construct plural of migdal, whereas the Septuagint reflects a Piel participle megaddelot, yielding or growing.
notes.6:4: Hebrew nidgalot, rendered armies with banners and repeated in 6:10, is a Niphal feminine plural participle from degel, banner, referring to bannered hosts, though some connect it to an Akkadian cognate meaning splendid sights or celestial bodies.
notes.6:5: Hebrew hirhibuni, they have overpowered me, is the Hiphil perfect of rahab, conveying overwhelming or unsettling force; unlike 4:1, the Masoretic Text here reads from Gilead without Mount.
notes.6:12: This verse is notoriously difficult, literally reading I did not know, my soul placed me the chariots of my noble people; the two-word Masoretic phrase ammi nadiv is also sometimes understood as a personal name, Amminadib, or as my kinsman, a prince.
notes.7:1: The Hebrew phrase "mah-techezu" can mean either "Why do you gaze..." or "What do you see...". "The two camps" translates the dual noun with the definite article, which may also refer to the place name Mahanaim.
notes.7:6: "Tresses" translates a Hebrew plural noun ("rehatim") that means "watering troughs" or "channels" elsewhere (Gen 30:38; Exod 2:16), used here poetically for flowing curls of hair.
notes.7:10: The Hebrew abruptly shifts from second-person "your palate" to first-person "for my beloved," suggesting a quick change of speaker. The rare participle "dovev" ("gliding over") can also mean "gently moving," and the Masoretic Text reads "those who sleep" ("yeshenim") rather than "teeth" as in some ancient versions.
notes.7:12: The plural Hebrew noun "kefarim" may mean either "villages" (from "kafar") or "henna blossoms" (from "kofer," as in 4:13).
notes.8:2: The Piel imperfect form "telammedeni" is morphologically ambiguous and may be read as third-person feminine singular ("she who used to teach me," referring to the mother) or second-person masculine singular ("you would teach me," referring to the beloved).
notes.8:4: Unlike the parallel adjurations in 2:7 and 3:5, which use the oath particle "im," the Masoretic Text here uses the interrogative "mah" ("why") rhetorically as an emphatic prohibition ("do not"), pairing the Hiphil and Polel stems of the verb "ur" ("rouse" and "awaken").
notes.8:6: The compound word "shalhevetyah" is written as a single word in the Masoretic Text and literally means "a flame of the LORD" (using the shortened divine name Yah), which may also function as a Hebrew superlative idiom meaning "a blazing flame." "Bolts" translates "reshafim," referring to fiery flashes, bolts, or sparks.
notes.8:7: The final Hebrew clause literally reads "scorning, they would scorn him" (an emphatic Qal infinitive absolute plus finite verb with an impersonal plural subject); the masculine pronoun "lo" ("him") may also refer to "it," namely the wealth offered.
